articles.title: Testing hypothesized neural substrates with lesions
articles.content: Correlative neuroimaging generates anatomical hypotheses causally testable by lesion studies. Regionally weighted lesion volume-deficit regression - comparing slopes of behavioural dependence on damage inside vs outside a hypothesized neural substrate - and compartmental volume comparisons inheriting the same logic have been widely employed for this task, but without analytical examination or empirical validation of the underlying methodology. Here we show analytically that this approach does not provide a valid test of whether the hypothesized compartment identifies the true substrate. To illustrate the empirical consequences, we conduct semi-synthetic simulations using 4119 ischaemic lesions, modelling behavioural deficits dependent on a global lesion attribute, on widely investigated distributed cortical networks and white matter tracts, or on a right frontal substrate of fluid intelligence previously identified by multivariate methods. We apply regionally weighted regression with each hypothesized compartment as the target over 5000 iterations spanning multiple realistic noise levels. Where the hypothesized target is not the true substrate, we find spuriously significant dependence despite definitionally absent anatomical specificity; adjustment for lesion volume attenuates or exacerbates the observed bias dependent on the chosen target. Conversely, where the target is the true substrate, lesion volume correction universally reduces already poor sensitivity. Our analysis potentially explains common discrepancies across localisation studies, and highlights the necessity of multivariate approaches that explicitly model lesion and substrate anatomy at finely resolved spatial scales.
articles.author: Bey, P., Ruffle, J. K., Nelson, A., Chan, E., Cipolotti, L., Nachev, P.

articles.title: Historeceptomics Profiling of Ketamine
articles.content: Ketamine elicits distinctive neuropsychiatric phenotypes from a complex and as yet elusive mechanism of action. Here, we applied an updated Historeceptomics approach to identify molecular targets and brain tissues that may contribute to its antidepressant, analgesic, and dissociative effects. Historeceptomics generates multidimensional target-tissue fingerprints by integrating drug-target activity with tissue-specific target expression, providing an anatomic profile of drug action. The results suggest that ketamine activity on NMDA receptors in the prefrontal and cingulate cortices and the amygdala may contribute to ketamine improvements in social functioning for MDD. However, this same receptor-tissue activity may invoke hallucinatory effects at higher intensity or with engagement of additional brain regions. The central nervous system (CNS) fingerprint for ketamine was compared with those of other psychoactive drugs, showing overlap with fingerprints from other antidepressant, hallucinogenic, and analgesic drugs. Some ketamine effects may be traced to specific enantiomers or metabolites of ketamine. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms by which ketamine elicits its unique phenotype and demonstrate the utility of using Historeceptomics to understand complex drug action.
articles.author: Rosenn, E., Agnor, H., Fuller, J., Cardozo, T.

articles.title: Temporal regularity shapes thalamocortical responses and deviance sensitivity in the anesthetized rat
articles.content: The brain uses regularities in the sensory environment to anticipate upcoming events, but whether predictions about stimulus identity and timing rely on dissociable neural mechanisms remains unclear. Here, we independently manipulated the temporal structure of acoustic sequences (rhythmic vs. jittered) and stimulus deviance of sequence elements (deviants vs. standards) while recording local field potentials (LFPs) and multiunit activity (AMUA) simultaneously from ventral and dorsal medial geniculate body (MGB) and cortical layers in 9 female anesthetized rats. Temporal structure robustly modulated neural responses throughout the auditory thalamocortical system. LFP responses were stronger for jittered than rhythmic stimulation across all layers of both primary and non-primary auditory cortex, with effects spanning early and later poststimulus intervals. AMUA responses showed a complementary temporal-predictability effect in both dorsal and ventral MGB, with stronger responses to jittered than rhythmic stimuli. In contrast, stimulus deviance effects were strongly dependent on temporal context and recording site. Deviant standard differences were enhanced under jittered stimulation in cortex and in early MGB responses, whereas later MGB responses showed a context dependent reversal. Finally, AMUA based Granger analyses revealed sustained jitter specific directed influences from both dorsal and ventral MGB toward multiple cortical layers during the poststimulus period. Together, these findings demonstrate that temporal regularity robustly modulates auditory thalamocortical responses and is associated with changes in directed interactions between thalamus and cortex. Responses to stimulus deviance, in turn, depend on temporal context and recording site. These findings reveal distinct but interacting neural signatures of temporal regularity and stimulus deviance in the auditory thalamocortical system.
articles.author: AN, H., Peng, F., Kotz, S. A., Schnupp, J. W. H., Auksztulewicz, R.

articles.title: Adaptive behaviors emerge from Hebbian-like plasticity through flexible attractors
articles.content: Adaptive behavior is commonly framed as an optimization problem, in which organisms learn to maximize reward. Here we show that simple networks with local, Hebbian-like learning rules, which have no reward objective, nonetheless reproduce hallmark features of animal reward-seeking when placed in closed-loop environments where rewards arrive as ordinary sensory input. Six canonical local learning rules were tested under these conditions, and despite most rules being designed for unsupervised representation learning, all rules learned to seek out signal. However, at the parameters tested, only one rule, prospective configuration, robustly captured all of a set of tested phenomena: reward-magnitude-dependent learning rates, probability matching, memory retention across contexts, and switching between exploration and exploitation with heavy-tailed statistics. In these networks, actions that produce input become self-sustaining states (attractors) of network dynamics. Attractors reside in an activity-weight space and mediate behaviors, and adapt to their environments rather than being fixed properties of the networks. These flexible geometries provide a parsimonious account of how heavy-tailed runs of repeated choices, which resemble Levy flights seen in foraging, also change with the environment. A single framework then makes predictions about behavior and neural population geometries that can be used to investigate the learning dynamics of the brain.
articles.author: Li, C., Brenner, J. W., Ye, H., du Pont, B., Kudarauskas, M., Aloor, J., Duan, C. A., Chen, J. A., Erlich, J. C.

articles.title: Sex-dependent gating of astrocyte-driven nociceptive plasticity
articles.content: Sex differences in pain are well established, yet how nociceptive processing is differentially regulated across sexes remains poorly understood. Here, we show that spinal astrocytes provide pathway-specific control of acute nociceptive synaptic plasticity in rats. Chemogenetic activation of distinct astrocytic G-protein-coupled receptor pathways induced synaptic depression or potentiation at spinal nociceptive synapses in males, but failed to evoke detectable plasticity in females. Despite this lack of astrocyte-induced synaptic plasticity, females developed mechanical hypersensitivity comparable to males, revealing a dissociation between synaptic plasticity and pain-related behavior. Gonadectomy prevented astrocyte-induced plasticity in males, whereas testosterone treatment enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in ovariectomized females. Females exhibited more prominent perineuronal net labeling, and enzymatic degradation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in females. Together, these findings identify hormonal status and ECM organization as important determinants of the susceptibility of spinal nociceptive circuits to astrocyte-driven synaptic plasticity.
articles.author: Klinger, L., Uhrik, L., Ravagnan, E., Holzinger, R., Trofimova, L., Kurija, D., Siegert, A. S. M., Ada, S., Waidhofer-Soellner, P., Schmidt, M., Drdla-Schutting, R.

articles.title: Rage bait: a neurofunctional signature of moral outrage elicited by social media
articles.content: Moral outrage is ubiquitous online, with powerful emotional and motivational consequences for social life. Combining naturalistic fMRI during exposure to short-form social-media videos depicting moral violations with predictive modeling, we developed a neurofunctional signature of subjective moral outrage (MONS) in discovery/validation (n=80/30) cohorts. MONS predicted experienced outrage and punishment tendencies across cohorts. Positive predictive weights encompassed regions implicated in mentalizing, threat detection and action initiation (precuneus, posterior cingulate, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, cerebellum), whereas negative weights involved valuation and behavioral flexibility systems (amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex). Across 11 datasets (n=478), MONS captured anger and disgust but was dissociable from general negative affect and affective arousal. Notably, MONS did not predict perceived moral wrongness in conventional moral judgment paradigms, suggesting that moral outrage is not reducible to more cognitive moral evaluation. Findings provide a moral outrage neurofunctional model that delineates its relationship to other affective states and distinguishes it from traditional moral judgment.
articles.author: Gan, X., Zhang, R., Zhou, F., Wagels, L., Jiang, H., Wang, J., Qing, Y., Yang, X., He, J., Zheng, Z., Xu, T., Mathiak, K., Jiang, B., Yao, D., Becker, B.

articles.title: Expanded representation and function of PDF neurons in the mosquito circadian network
articles.content: Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can transmit pathogens when they bite humans, their preferred hosts, and this host-seeking drive is tightly gated by time of day. Daily rhythms depend on the molecular clock and communication among clock neurons, yet mosquito circadian network organization remains poorly understood. Using a mosquito-specific PERIOD antibody, we mapped the putative clock network of Aedes aegypti and found that neurons expressing the neuropeptide Pigment-Dispersing Factor (PDF) make up a much larger proportion of clock neurons compared to other insects, indicating a divergent network organization. PDF neurons are required for normal rhythms across insects, but whether their importance scales with their abundance in the network is unknown. We therefore tested the functional role of this expanded PDF neuron population in mosquitoes: we show that electrically silencing Aedes aegypti PDF neurons abolished the separation of daily activity into morning and evening peaks and led to misaligned clock protein rhythms across circadian neurons, even under entraining light-dark cycles. Thus, in a network built around an unusually large PDF population, PDF neuron activity plays an outsized role in behavioral timing and network synchrony.
articles.author: Dong, L., Plank, A. V., Duvall, L. B.

articles.title: Common organization of collective dynamics across divergent self-organized neural architectures
articles.content: Brain organoids and other model neuronal networks build synaptic circuits through self-organization, and different protocols yield markedly different architectures, letting us test how collective dynamics depend on large-scale organization. We compared organoids of layered cortical-like structure against networks of cell-body clusters joined by axonal cables, quantifying the reproducible patterns of population activity in each. Bursts occurred in both architectures and comprised several collective patterns in each, so no single recurring template describes them. Recurrent activation sequences capture only part of this organization, sequence participation is graded, and neurons that rarely join a sequence still contribute to the shared dynamics. The patterns also pick out overlapping neuronal groups with propagation-like spatial order. Although the patterns differed between tissue models, their organization was conserved, and remained unchanged under pharmacological increases in network activity. Recurrent sequences therefore represent one manifestation of a broader collective organization that emerges across distinct self-organized neural architectures.
articles.author: Zhao, Z., Yang, L., Nemenman, I., Levchenko, A.

articles.title: Preprocessing Determines Whether Fractal Biomarkers Detect Neurodegeneration: A Systematic Evaluation Across Five fMRI Pipelines
articles.content: Fractal analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been proposed for detecting altered neural dynamics in Alzheimers disease (AD), but the effect of preprocessing on these measurements is poorly constrained. We evaluated 229 ADNI3 participants (156 cognitively normal [CN], 60 mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and 13 AD) processed with five ENIGMA HALFpipe variants. Each scan contained 197 volumes (TR = 3.0 s) and 434 regional time series. The reported CN-AD effect varied 4.5-fold for the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) Hurst exponent and 13.1-fold for Sample Entropy; both measures met p < 0.05 only after aCompCor. Under aCompCor, mean H was 0.812 in CN, 0.827 in MCI, and 0.872 in AD (d = -1.40, p = 0.0003), whereas the other four DFA effects were approximately d = -0.31 to -0.40. A variance decomposition attributed 41.5% of total H variance to pipeline, 44.5% to participant, and 0.3% to diagnosis. Whole-brain analysis found higher H in AD across 16 of 18 networks, with 36 cortical regions surviving false-discovery-rate correction. Synthetic fractional Gaussian noise experiments confirmed monotonic DFA estimation at the available scan length. The small AD group makes all disease-effect estimates exploratory. These results show that preprocessing choice can determine whether fractal group differences are detectable and should therefore be treated as part of the biomarker definition.
articles.author: Chattopadhyay, T., Cen, H. S., Thomopoulos, S. I., Volkov, A., Maximov, Y., Motter, A. D., Tankesly, H., Ruekgauer, A. H., Khopade, A., Gabitov, I., Thompson, P.

articles.title: Prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling promotes maladaptive plasticity of direct pathway striatal projection neurons
articles.content: As Parkinson's disease (PD) progresses and nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) neuron degeneration worsens, DA replacement therapies shift from restoring motor function to evoking dyskinesia. How disease progression mediates this transition remains poorly understood. Here, we optimized a 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA) model that reliably generates multiple severities of DA axon denervation within the striatum of individual mice. We identify a critical denervation threshold at which direct-pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs), which are key drivers of dyskinesia become pathologically hyperresponsive to DA. Using slice electrophysiology, we establish that denervation-induced increase in intrinsic excitability is insufficient to explain the aberrant response of dSPNs to DA. We further demonstrate using genetic and chemogenetic manipulations that prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling drives the pathological transformation of dSPNs cell-autonomously, and that sustained Gs-coupled metabotropic receptor signaling in dSPNs is sufficient to both prevent and reverse it. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how PD progression renders striatal circuits vulnerable to DA-evoked motor complications and identify sustained signaling by Gs-coupled receptors as a potential avenue for preventing or reversing denervation-induced maladaptive striatal plasticity.

articles.title: Influence of out-of-plane electric fields in an ex vivo model of transcranial electrical stimulation
articles.content: Objective. Electrical stimulation is the most commonly used modality for neuromodulation, with a number of clinical and scientific applications. Although the basic mechanisms of neural activation by electrical stimulation are well understood, important questions remain regarding neural responses to diffuse electric fields such as those generated by transcranial electrical stimulation. For such diffuse fields, the orientation of the electric field with respect to the neurons being stimulated matters, but previous ex vivo brain slice studies–commonly used to study how neurons respond to external electric fields-have only considered electric fields applied in the plane of the slice. Approach. We used two electrode arrays–one oriented parallel and the other perpendicular to coronal brain slices–to generate electric fields oriented orthogonally to the slice as well as along the cortical column. We measured responses in Layer 5 of the somatosensory cortex using several 2-electrode stimulation configurations, while also varying the distance between the electrodes and the slice. Main results. Electrode patterns generating a large electric field component orthogonal to the slice evoked the largest neural responses at every electrode-slice distance. Moreover, neural thresholds were >5× lower for electric fields orthogonal to the slice compared to electric fields along the cortical column. Significance. These results provide a better understanding of the brain slice as a model for noninvasive stimulation and could lead to new electrode configurations for efficient transcranial neural stimulation.
articles.author: Yuhyun Lee, Vishal Jain, Yuxin Guo, Maysamreza Chamanzar, Pulkit Grover and Mats Forssell

articles.title: AIM-STAGE: a self-supervised framework via adaptive interval-aware multi-kernel calibration and spectro-temporal exploration for few-shot EEG staging
articles.content: Objective. Learning discriminative and generalizable representations from electroencephalography (EEG) signals with limited annotations remains a key challenge in automatic sleep staging. Supervised deep models depend on large-scale expert labels, yet sleep annotation is costly and time-consuming. Existing self-supervised methods often underuse EEG spectral-temporal structure and adopt fixed negative-sample strategies, which are poorly suited to the continuous transitions and ambiguous boundaries between sleep stages. This study proposes AIM-STAGE, a self-supervised representation learning framework for limited-label EEG sleep staging. Approach. AIM-STAGE comprises three modules. (1) Spectral-temporal exploration. maps EEG segments into the time-frequency domain through the short-time Fourier transform, jointly extracting log-power and cross-channel phase difference to characterize frequency-band activity and phase dynamics. (2) Local-global hybrid encoding. uses a CNN-Transformer encoder, in which convolutional residual modules capture local spectro-temporal patterns and a bottleneck Transformer models long-range dependencies. (3) Adaptive interval-aware multi-kernel calibration. Employs multiple Gaussian kernels and dynamic weighting to synthesize informative negative representations, improving view consistency and inter-sample separability. Main results. AIM-STAGE was evaluated on SLEEP-2013, SLEEP-2018, SHHS-D, and SHHS-H against ContraWR, DFformer, EEG2Rep, EEGPT, Superlet-MAE, and a supervised baseline across 1%–15% labels. Accuracy improved from 88.67% to 92.04% on SLEEP-2013, and AIM-STAGE outperformed all baselines on all four datasets with higher kappa, macro- 1, and balanced accuracy, including on the pathological SHHS-D cohort. Ablation confirmed the contributions of the bottleneck Transformer, positional embeddings, physiology-informed augmentation, and calibration loss. Per-stage analysis showed that N1 is the most difficult stage, with 1 ranging from 0.003–0.046, and adding EOG and EMG markedly improved its precision, recall, and 1. Significance. AIM-STAGE offers an interpretable and label-efficient self-supervised solution for EEG sleep staging, improving robustness and stage discriminability under scarce-label conditions while reducing dependence on manual annotation.
articles.author: Yijia Liu, Tianhao Liu, Jun Yuan, Yunfeng Li, Xingyu Liu, Xiaoqing Wang, Tiantian Ma, Liyang Bi, Xiaozhu Lin, Nasrollah Moghadam Charkari, Hossein Ganjidoust, Titus Alfred Makudali Msagati and Qianjin Guo

articles.title: Decoding attempted handwritten characters based on temporal endovascular neural features
articles.content: Objective. We evaluated temporal neural features for motor decoding using a minimally-invasive endovascular brain–computer singular: interface (BCI). We hypothesised that relatively long compound movements generate distinct patterns of neural activity that are encoded by temporal features. Approach. A single participant implanted with the Stentrode endovascular BCI attempted to hand write English characters, which were then classified offline and online based on the recorded brain activity. The input to the model was a one-dimensional trajectory of high-gamma power, summed across all channels to isolate the effect of temporal information on decoding performance. Main results. A small number of classes across multiple months was reliably decoded, showing that temporal decoding could identify stable patterns of brain activity associated with each handwriting movement. Across four online sessions, where each session contained 20–30 trials/character and 80–180 rest trials, the best performing (3-class) model achieved a mean rest recall of 87% as well as character recall and precision of 65% and 59%, respectively. These results showed that attempted handwriting can be used in an online multi-class selection BCI and that temporal neural features capture the internal user context. Linear warping of trials to minimise temporal variability, where all trials were modified to have the same duration, led to significantly increased decoding performance compared to classifying raw trials. Significance. The results from our participant showed that decoding brain activity based on the differences between feature trajectories across time can be an effective strategy for discriminating different movements. Therefore, BCIs may be able to use temporal information to reduce their spatial footprint, likely making them less invasive. Overall, our study shows that further investigation of temporal decoding across multiple participants and other recording modalities is warranted. Strategies for automatic temporal alignment are likely to further improve the performance of these systems.

articles.content: Motor cortical high-gamma oscillations (60-90 Hz) occur at movement onset and are spatially focused over the contralateral primary motor cortex. articles.title: NIRS-BIDS: Brain Imaging Data Structure Extended to Near-Infrared Spectroscopy
articles.content: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is an increasingly popular neuroimaging technique that measures cortical hemodynamic activity in a non-invasive and portable fashion. Although the fNIRS community has been successful in disseminating open-source processing tools and a standard file format (SNIRF), reproducible research and sharing of fNIRS data amongst researchers has been hindered by a lack of standards and clarity over how study data should be organized and stored.
